summary: This memo specifies a URI scheme for identifying PKCS #11 objects stored in PKCS #11 tokens, and for identifying tokens, slots, or libraries. The scheme is based on how those items are already described by attributes in PKCS #11.

plainLanguage.summary: Some secure keys are stored in special hardware. This gives a web-like address for pointing at a specific key on a specific device.

questions: how to refer to a key on a token
how to identify a key on a token
subtitle: A URI form for pointing at a key, certificate, token, slot or library behind the PKCS #11 API.

tldr.problem: Programs that use PKCS #11 cryptographic tokens have no common text identifier for a stored object, a token, a slot or a Cryptoki library, so each tool invents its own way to name them in configuration files and command lines.
tldr.mechanism: The pkcs11 URI scheme writes the attributes PKCS #11 already uses (token label, object label, type, id, slot and library details) as semicolon-separated pairs in the path, with optional query attributes for the PIN source and for module lookup.
tldr.outcome: The scheme is registered as Permanent in the URI scheme registry. It is meant for identifying existing items, not for creating new objects or tokens.

today: RFC 7512 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It moved the pkcs11 scheme from the Provisional to the Permanent URI scheme registry.

sections.title: What the PKCS #11 URI Names
sections.content:
PKCS #11 defines an API called Cryptoki for devices that hold cryptographic information and perform cryptographic functions. Applications see each device as a cryptographic token. This RFC adds a common identifier so an application or library can be told which stored object, token, slot or Cryptoki library to use.

A PKCS #11 URI can identify storage objects (a certificate, a data object, or a public, private or secret key), tokens, slots and libraries. It cannot identify other PKCS #11 objects such as a hardware feature or a mechanism. It is not meant to create new objects or tokens: it only identifies and works with existing ones.

The scheme uses the scheme, path and query components of RFC 3986. It has no naming authority in the path, because an authority could not be mapped to PKCS #11 API elements, and it does not use the fragment component.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a building full of locked lockers. This gives every locker, and every locker room, a short written address so a program knows exactly which one to open.

sections.title: Scheme Syntax and Path Attributes
sections.content:
A PKCS #11 URI starts with pkcs11:, followed by a path of attribute-value pairs separated by semicolons, optionally followed by ? and a query. The path may be empty. Each attribute may appear at most once in the path.

Path attributes map to PKCS #11 names: token, manufacturer, serial and model describe the token; slot-description, slot-manufacturer and slot-id describe the slot; library-manufacturer, library-description and library-version describe the library; object, type and id describe a storage object. Vendor-specific attributes are allowed and must not clash with existing names.

Text values SHOULD be encoded as UTF-8 and then percent-encoded where needed. The id attribute is the exception: it can hold non-textual data, so it SHOULD be entirely percent-encoded rather than treated as UTF-8. The slash, the question mark and the hash character MUST be percent-encoded in the path so generic URI parsers do not split it. A consumer that meets values PKCS #11 itself would not accept MUST refuse the URI as invalid.

The library-version value has the form M.N, where both numbers are one byte in size and the major number is REQUIRED. A bare M means major M and minor 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is a list of clues like label, kind and serial number, each written as name=value. The more clues you give, the fewer lockers match.

sections.title: Query Attributes: PINs and Modules
sections.content:
The query part carries attributes that help retrieve the item. pin-source says where to find the normal user's token PIN, and pin-value supplies the PIN directly. module-name and module-path adjust how PKCS #11 providers are located.

The format of pin-source is implementation specific, but the RFC lists rules to follow in order. If the value is a URI (such as file:, https: or another PKCS #11 URI), treat it as an object holding the PIN. If it contains |<absolute-command-path>, read the PIN from that command's output. Otherwise interpret it in an implementation-dependent way. A URI containing both pin-source and pin-value SHOULD be refused as invalid.

module-name is a case-insensitive module name without system-specific affixes such as a lib prefix or .so suffix. module-path is an absolute path to a module or to a directory of modules, and a relative path SHOULD be rejected. Using both in one URI SHOULD be avoided, and a consumer MAY refuse either one.

Both pin-value and the module attributes have security consequences, covered in Section 6 of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra notes after the question mark tell the program where to find the password and which helper software to use. Putting the password right in the address is risky, like writing it on the locker.

sections.title: Matching and Comparing URIs
sections.content:
A URI may identify four kinds of things (objects, tokens, slots or libraries), so the consumer needs to know from context which kind it wants. Matching works by narrowing: an attribute that is absent from the path matches everything, each extra attribute narrows the result, and an empty path matches everything accessible. An unrecognized path attribute, including a vendor attribute, SHOULD give an empty set of matches, while an unrecognized query attribute SHOULD be ignored.

Two URIs are equal if they are identical as character strings, or if they have the same set of attributes (order does not matter) and equal values. Most text attributes are compared as simple strings after case and percent-encoding normalization from RFC 3986. The id value is compared after all bytes are percent-encoded with uppercase hex digits A to F. library-version and slot-id are compared numerically.

Slot IDs are assigned by Cryptoki and are not guaranteed to be stable across module initializations, so slot-id is likely to cause usability issues except where a library provides stable IDs. A consumer generating URIs MAY offer URI template support (RFC 6570).
sections.plainLanguage: Finding a locker is like a game of twenty questions: every clue you add rules out more lockers. Two addresses count as the same if they give the same clues, even in a different order.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows URIs for each kind of target. The simplest is an empty pkcs11:. A public key can be named by label and type alone, using the default token. A private key usually adds pin-source in the query; there / stays unencoded because the query component is separated by ? from the path.

Other examples identify a certificate in a software token by token, manufacturer, model, object, type, id and serial (an empty serial matches only an empty serial number), a token without any object, a slot by slot-description, and a library by manufacturer, description and version. Spaces are percent-encoded, and the hash character in a token name MUST be percent-encoded. A semicolon inside a value must also be percent-encoded, and a non-ASCII character such as a small A with acute is UTF-8 encoded and then percent-encoded as %C3%A1.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show addresses of different sizes, from a vague one that means any locker to a very exact one that names a single key.

sections.title: Internationalization
sections.content:
PKCS #11 does not define a canonical form for its UTF-8 strings, so unnormalized text can cause false matches and false mismatches. Because PKCS #11 items are local and local security is assumed, the RFC treats these as usability and interoperability concerns.

It is RECOMMENDED that applications creating objects or labeling tokens use only US-ASCII characters for labels. If that is not possible, labels SHOULD be normalized to Normalization Form C (NFC). The same advice applies to the names of libraries, slots and tokens. Applications MAY convert names to a chosen normalization form before comparing, since existing names may predate these recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: The same letter can sometimes be typed in more than one way inside a computer. Using plain letters, or one agreed way to write the fancy ones, keeps the search from missing a match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the general URI security considerations of RFC 3986 and picks out three. There is no guarantee the same URI will always identify the same object, token, slot or library in the future. Accepting module-name or module-path can allow loading arbitrary code into a process. And a URI may sit in world-readable command-line arguments or public configuration files, so pin-value should only be used if the URI string is protected as strongly as the PIN itself.

PKCS #11 authenticates users to tokens but gives no means to authenticate devices to users, so it relies on local and physical security. For that reason the usual normalization and confusable-script concerns do not arise, though normalizing to NFC is still advised when non-ASCII characters are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing a password inside the address is like taping your locker combination to the door. Letting a stranger pick the helper software is like letting them hand you the keys to run.
